name: Collaborative Editor (Google Docs)
description: Design a real-time collaborative document editor like Google Docs. Covers CRDT/OT conflict resolution, cursor presence, WebSocket communication, and document persistence.

learnSteps.title: Real-Time WebSocket Communication
learnSteps.description: Clients maintain persistent WebSocket connections to the Collaboration Server. Each keystroke generates an operation (insert/delete at position) that is sent to the server in real-time. The Load Balancer uses consistent hashing on document ID to route all editors of the same document to the same server instance, reducing cross-server coordination.

learnSteps.title: CRDT-Based Conflict Resolution
learnSteps.description: The system uses a CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type) — specifically a sequence CRDT like Yjs or Automerge — to resolve concurrent edits without a central lock. Each character has a unique ID based on (clientID, sequence). Concurrent insertions at the same position are deterministically ordered by ID. The CRDT state is cached in Redis for fast document loads.

learnSteps.title: Cross-Server Operation Sync
learnSteps.description: When a document has editors connected to different server instances (due to scaling or reconnects), operations must sync across servers. The Operation Sync Bus (Kafka) broadcasts operations for each document. Each server subscribes to topics for documents it is hosting, applies remote operations to its local CRDT state, and pushes updates to connected clients.

learnSteps.title: Document Persistence and Version History
learnSteps.description: The CRDT state is periodically snapshotted to PostgreSQL (every N operations or every 30 seconds). Full document snapshots are stored in S3 for version history and recovery. PostgreSQL stores metadata (document ID, owner, permissions, last modified). On document open, the server loads the latest CRDT snapshot from Redis (cache hit) or PostgreSQL (cache miss), then replays any operations from Kafka since the snapshot.

chaosScenarios.name: Collaboration Server Crash
chaosScenarios.description: One of the 30 WebSocket servers crashes, dropping the ~33k live editing sessions that consistent hashing had pinned to it
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Reconnect storm as ~33k clients rehash to surviving servers within seconds. New owners load CRDT state from Redis and replay Kafka operations since the last snapshot. Edit latency spikes for affected documents; unsnapshotted ops remain safe in the Kafka log.
mitigationSteps: Clients reconnect with jittered exponential backoff to flatten the storm
Surviving servers warm CRDT state from Redis before accepting edits
Replay per-document Kafka offsets since the last snapshot to restore unpersisted ops
Auto-scale a replacement instance and let consistent hashing rebalance

chaosScenarios.name: Sync Bus Network Partition
chaosScenarios.description: A network partition cuts a subset of collaboration servers off from the Kafka operation bus while their client WebSockets stay healthy
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Editors of the same document connected to servers on opposite sides stop seeing each other's edits; local editing keeps working. CRDT semantics guarantee deterministic convergence once the partition heals and buffered operations flush, but presence and cursors are stale for the duration.
mitigationSteps: Surface a degraded-sync indicator to clients instead of failing edits
Buffer outbound operations locally with producer retries
On heal, drain the backlog in order and let CRDT merge converge replicas
Page if consumer lag has not returned to baseline within 5 minutes

chaosScenarios.name: CRDT State Cache Loss
chaosScenarios.description: The 128GB Redis cache holding hot CRDT document state fails completely
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Active sessions keep editing from in-memory server state, but every new document open becomes a cache miss: load latency jumps from ~50ms to seconds (PostgreSQL snapshot read plus Kafka replay), and the doc-open stampede pressures the 500-connection DB pool.
mitigationSteps: Fail document opens over to PostgreSQL snapshots with rate limiting to protect the pool
Force snapshots from in-memory server state to shrink replay windows
Restore Redis and warm it with the most recently active documents first
Hold non-essential batch jobs off PostgreSQL until cache hit rate recovers

bottleneckProgression.description: Periodic CRDT snapshot writes across thousands of hot documents saturate the 500-connection PostgreSQL pool
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Batch snapshot writes, add PgBouncer pooling, lengthen the snapshot interval for low-activity documents

bottleneckProgression.description: Hot documents concentrate operations on a few of the 64 Kafka partitions; consumer lag delays cross-server sync
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Increase partition count, batch and compress small operations, shed presence/cursor traffic before document edits

bottleneckProgression.description: Per-connection buffers plus CRDT metadata (tombstones, per-character IDs) exhaust the 32GB heap on busy servers
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale out the fleet, run CRDT tombstone compaction, offload presence to a separate lightweight service

expectedIssues.title: Hot Document Pinned to One Server
expectedIssues.description: Consistent hashing routes every editor of a document to a single server, so a document with hundreds of concurrent editors cannot be spread out and saturates that instance with a broadcast per keystroke
expectedIssues.mitigation: Cap concurrent editors per document, coalesce broadcasts on a 50-100ms tick, demote overflow viewers to read-only follower mode

expectedIssues.title: CRDT Tombstone Accumulation
expectedIssues.description: Long-lived, heavily edited documents accumulate deletion tombstones and per-character metadata, inflating CRDT state in Redis and server memory far beyond the visible text size
expectedIssues.mitigation: Periodic state compaction during quiet periods; archive cold history to S3 revisions

expectedIssues.title: Reconnect Storm After Restart
expectedIssues.description: A rolling deploy or LB change drops large batches of WebSocket connections at once; simultaneous reconnects plus CRDT state loads spike server CPU and Redis traffic
expectedIssues.mitigation: Connection draining on deploys, client-side jittered backoff, reconnect admission control at the load balancer

expectedIssues.title: Snapshot Lag Slows Document Opens
expectedIssues.description: If snapshotting falls behind (DB pressure or failed jobs), opening a document requires replaying a long Kafka operation tail, turning sub-second opens into multi-second waits
expectedIssues.mitigation: Alert on snapshot age; prioritize snapshots for documents with the longest replay tails

expectedIssues.title: Operation Loss Beyond Kafka Retention
expectedIssues.description: Operations between snapshots live only in Kafka (168h retention); a document whose snapshots fail silently for longer than retention loses acknowledged edits permanently
expectedIssues.mitigation: Monitor per-document snapshot success, alert well before the retention window closes, keep S3 revision backups

metrics.name: sync_bus_consumer_lag
metrics.description: Kafka lag on per-document operation topics

metrics.name: snapshot_age_seconds
metrics.description: Max time since last persisted CRDT snapshot across hot documents

steps: Confirm instance loss via LB health checks and the connection-count drop
Verify client backoff is engaged — reconnect rate trending down, not sawtoothing
Watch CRDT cache hit rate: rehashed documents should warm from Redis, not PostgreSQL
Confirm Kafka replay lag for rehashed documents returns to zero
Scale out replacement capacity before declaring all-clear
Identify hot partitions and the documents behind them
Shed presence/cursor updates to prioritize document operations
Scale consumer threads on the affected servers
If sustained, expand the partition count during a low-traffic window
Enable doc-open rate limiting to protect the PostgreSQL pool
Force snapshots from in-memory state on all servers to shrink replay windows
Restore or replace the Redis cluster and warm the hottest documents first
Lift rate limits once cache hit rate exceeds 80%

decisions.title: CRDT over Operational Transformation
decisions.context: Concurrent edits from up to 1M users must converge deterministically without a central lock or transform sequencer
decisions.decision: Use a sequence CRDT (Yjs/Automerge-style) where each character carries a unique (clientID, sequence) identity and concurrent inserts order deterministically
consequences: No central transformation server in the hot path
Offline and partitioned edits merge cleanly on reconnect
Per-character metadata and tombstones inflate document state, requiring compaction

decisions.title: Document-Sticky Routing via Consistent Hashing
decisions.context: Broadcasting edits between co-editors is cheapest when they share a process
decisions.decision: The load balancer consistent-hashes on document ID so all editors of a document land on one collaboration server
consequences: Most edits fan out in-memory with no cross-server hop
Hot documents cannot be spread across servers
A server crash concentrates a reconnect storm on its rehashed documents

decisions.title: Kafka as Durable Operation Log
decisions.context: Edits acknowledged to users must survive a server crash that happens between periodic snapshots
decisions.decision: Publish every operation to a 7-day-retention Kafka bus that doubles as the cross-server sync channel and the replay source on recovery
consequences: Snapshot plus replay-since-offset gives bounded recovery time
Cross-server sync inherits Kafka's ~2-5ms hop latency
The retention window becomes a hard durability boundary if snapshots silently fail

tradeoffs.choice: Acknowledge edits after Kafka publish, before any database snapshot
tradeoffs.cost: Durability between snapshots rests entirely on the Kafka log

tradeoffs.choice: Pin each document to one server
tradeoffs.benefit: In-memory fanout and minimal cross-server coordination
tradeoffs.cost: Viral documents create uneven load that autoscaling cannot smooth

tradeoffs.choice: Carry full CRDT metadata per character
tradeoffs.benefit: Conflict-free, lock-free merges in any order
tradeoffs.cost: Document state several times larger than the visible text

alternatives.name: Central OT Sequencer
alternatives.description: Operational Transformation with a single per-document sequencer that transforms and orders all operations
alternatives.prosVsCons: Smaller document state and a mature model, but the sequencer is a per-document availability and scaling chokepoint
alternatives.whyNotChosen: CRDT removes central coordination and handles offline merges without server-side transform logic

alternatives.name: Pessimistic Section Locking
alternatives.description: Lock paragraphs or sections so only one user edits a region at a time
alternatives.prosVsCons: Trivial consistency, but blocks simultaneous character-level co-editing
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Real-time character-level collaboration is the product requirement

alternatives.name: Database as Sync Channel
alternatives.description: Persist every operation to PostgreSQL and have servers poll or LISTEN/NOTIFY for changes
alternatives.prosVsCons: Fewer moving parts, but 200k ops/sec of tiny writes overwhelms the database and polling adds latency
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Kafka absorbs the operation firehose with millisecond fanout and replayable history
